Age of Reckoning · A playable brief

Power Card

Vote or Fade Away

You're in your early 20s. Rent is up, gas is up, the job board is a graveyard, and a war plus a tariff storm are squeezing everything at once. The boss feeding on all of it is called The Fade — and it wins every time young people decide their vote doesn't matter. Sixteen battles. Three weapons. One Election Day. Play the brief. Beat the boss. Keep the future — and fight for the one your generation gets to shape.

The sound of hope: this isn't a doom game. It's a dawn game. Every informed strike is a step toward work that pays, leaders chosen by the people they serve, and a generation that refuses to fade — together.

Election Day · Tue Nov 3, 2026 16 battles · ~11 minutes No sign-up · No score saved
Check your registration

How it works: pick a fighter from the character sheets, then answer each battle with the most informed move. Right calls strike The Fade. Wrong calls teach you why — and cost you Hope. After every battle, you choose again: the band's character sheets come back up, and you send in whoever fits the next fight. Finish with The Fade at 40 HP or below to win. Death Blow: if The Fade drops under 15 HP, the fighter in the arena may get a golden one-shot Death Blow opening — land it and The Fade falls on the spot; miss it and that hero's Death Blow is spent for the game. The dice: a right answer earns an attack — swipe or tap the 3D d20, add your fighter's sheet bonuses and situational +2s, and beat The Fade's Defense or the blow only glances. A wrong answer lets The Fade counterattack your fighter's own hit points. Between battles you get one camp action: Priya's Healing Hands and the band's spells roll the three-sided die, and a landed Death Blow rolls the d6 for overkill. Fade Logic Engine: his taunts, excuses and label flips are drawn only from documented, non-partisan fact and history — tap his line in the arena for the correction and source. Hard Skill Level (on his sheet) raises his machine to 9–12, adds +2 Defense, unlocks his Fake News Gambit, and makes a Death Blow need a d6 roll of 3+ to finish him. The Power Card: facts charge it, courage plays it, and playing it is the strongest move the band owns besides a Death Blow.

1 · Read the fact → 2 · Answer from it → 3 · Roll to strike him → 4 · Break him to 40 HP by Battle 16 — or land a Death Blow

Why the facts? The fact is your weapon: a strike only happens because you got the fact right.

Choose your fighter

Three young players, three uncertain futures — the band's character sheets. Your fighter changes the story lines, not the facts — every battle below is drawn from the real brief: the 2026 U.S.–Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz, sweeping tariffs, and what the midterms actually control. And you choose again before every battle: hit “Next battle” after a fight and you'll land back here to send in the band member who fits the fight ahead. Tune each sheet, too: every ability score sits on a slider, but the caps are true to class — a warrior's strength tops out where a healer's never could, and the healer's magic and healing run higher than anyone's. The sliders are real, too: each sheet derives its combat numbers live — modifier = (stat − 8) ÷ 2, rounded, −2 to +4 — so tuning a stat moves the Attack, Damage and Defense numbers the dice use in the arena. And every sheet holds a fixed pool of build points: raise one score and the points come out of points you've banked by lowering others first — then straight out of that hero's highest other score. A sheet can change shape, but its total never grows. The Power Card lives on every sheet: facts charge it, courage plays it, and playing it is the strongest move the band owns besides a Death Blow.

Character sheet · Boss

The Fade

The Machinery of Manufactured War · Feeds on fear, apathy and amnesia

It does not argue — it drums. It does not persuade — it spins. It never plans to leave, and it happily fights you with weapons your own side handed to yesterday's allies. Starve the machine: beat the arguments, keep the receipts.

The Fade Logic Engine — documented moves only

Everything he says is built from non-partisan, checkable fact and documented history — never party framing. His trickery is the lesson: tap his line in the arena and the documented correction appears with its source.

  • (a) Rationale Carousel: his excuse rotates by hit points — threat → liberation → stability → “we're already there” — mirroring documented rationale rotation during the Iraq and Afghanistan occupations. Pattern documented in speeches, funding debates and occupation histories.
  • (b) Label Flips: the same fighters are relabelled as the decade demands — “freedom fighters” ↔ “terrorists,” ally ↔ tyrant. Drawn from the record: mujahideen armed in the 1980s who became al-Qaeda / the Taliban; Saddam backed in the 1980s, fought in 1991 and 2003; the Shah installed in 1953, whose fall produced the Iran of 1979 onward.
  • (c) Sound Bites: polished one-liners that say a checkable number wrong, loudly. Each distortion in this game is a distortion of a figure already in the brief — Hormuz volumes (EIA), tariff incidence (NY Fed / NBER), breakout and weaponization (IAEA) — and the correction is always shown.
  • (d) The War Chest: his jobs pitch — war sold as employment. The history underneath it is real (see The War Economy panel below), which is exactly why it works: contracts mean local jobs, so the spending defends itself politically. WWII mobilisation figures; F-35 supply chain across 45+ states; Eisenhower's 1961 farewell warning.
  • (e) The Debt Mountain: his complacency pitch — “Forty trillion and the sky hasn't fallen — relax,” “We owe it to ourselves, kid.” The documented correction: the federal debt is never actually paid down, only refinanced forever at whatever rate the market demands; net interest is now one of the largest single federal outlays, larger than the defense budget; and households carry the servicing bill through higher taxes and fees, inflation, and higher-for-longer rates (see The Debt Mountain panel below). U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data; CBO budget outlook; post-WWII debt-to-GDP record.

Lesson of The Fade

The pattern, in plain sight. In the 1980s the United States armed and praised Afghanistan's mujahideen as “freedom fighters” against the Soviets — the networks that legacy fed became al-Qaeda and the Taliban, who later turned those weapons and skills on the U.S. itself. In the same decade Washington backed Saddam Hussein's Iraq with intelligence and dual-use support during the Iran–Iraq war — then fought Saddam in 1991, and again in 2003. And in 1953 a U.S.-backed coup installed the Shah of Iran; the revolution that eventually threw him out made Iran the adversary of 2026.

The labels change with the decade — ally, freedom fighter, partner, tyrant, threat. The weapons remain. The Fade's whole game is hoping nobody keeps the receipts long enough to notice.

The War Economy

The jobs pitch is built on real history — which is why it is his strongest card. Wartime mobilisation has repeatedly bolstered U.S. employment and industrial output through government contracts: in World War II, U.S. unemployment fell from 14.7% in 1940 to 1.2% in 1944, and roughly 17 million civilian jobs were created on federal war contracts. That is precisely why the military-industrial machine has a constituency: contracts mean local jobs, and major programs deliberately distribute them — the F-35 supply chain spans 45+ states — so the spending defends itself politically, district by district.

The honest other half, always shown with it: that peak came with rationing and price controls; the national debt rose roughly five-fold from 1941 to 1945; and activity is not the same as welfare — building things to be destroyed is the classic broken-window point, output counted while wealth is spent. And the warning came from the top: Dwight Eisenhower — the general who won that war — used his 1961 farewell address to warn against the “military-industrial complex” and its “unwarranted influence.” The jobs were real. So was his warning.

Sources: U.S. WWII employment record (unemployment 1940–44; federal war-contract jobs); F-35 program supply-chain distribution (45+ states); U.S. federal debt 1941–45; Eisenhower farewell address, Jan 17, 1961.

The Debt Mountain

The stock itself: U.S. federal debt has ballooned past $40 trillion — and in the modern era it is never actually paid down. Maturing bonds are not retired; they are refinanced — rolled over, forever — at whatever interest rate the market demands that week. That is why the mountain connects directly to the cost-of-capital lesson: a growing supply of debt helps hold the term premium near ~1.07 points, the 10-year Treasury above 5%, and mortgages near ~7.4%. And net interest is now one of the largest single federal outlays — larger than the defense budget — and it buys nothing: no ships, no schools, just rent on past borrowing.

The stock in context — measured against the economy that has to carry it: gross federal debt stood at roughly 57% of GDP in 2001, when the government was running a surplus and the debt was shrinking relative to the economy. Two decades of decisions followed — the post-9/11 wars in Afghanistan and Iraq fought on borrowed money, tax cuts, the 2008 financial crisis, the pandemic, and now the Iran war. The ratio crossed 100% of GDP in the early 2010s and stands past 120% of GDP today. Passing debt down to future generations is not a new failure; it is the long-standing pattern this panel describes — each era's choices, financed by borrowing, become the next generation's inheritance. The ratio is what makes the inheritance visible.

The servicing bill is ultimately carried by households, through three pressure valves: (1) higher taxes and fees over time, as interest claims a growing share of every budget; (2) inflation, which quietly taxes savings and wages whenever the bill is eased with cheaper dollars; and (3) higher-for-longer interest rates, as the debt supply itself keeps borrowing costs up for every family financing a home or a car. The one historical exception proves the mechanism: after World War II the debt was never repaid either — it was outgrown and inflated down as a share of GDP across decades of growth. The burden shrank because the economy grew — which required the growth.

Sources: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data (total federal debt, $40T+); CBO Budget & Economic Outlook (net interest vs. defense outlays; debt held by the public); post-WWII debt-to-GDP record.

Your three weapons

Voting Arrows

Precision strikes. Every registered, informed ballot aimed at the exact lever of power — a race, a funding bill, a check on power — instead of sprayed into the void.

Axe of Freedom

Heavy swings that cut red tape and bad arguments: asking who built this crisis, who profits, and where's the proof? before anyone spends your future on it.

Sword of Youth

The long game. Young voters are the largest bloc that mostly stays home in midterms — which is exactly why The Fade fears you showing up, every cycle, in force.

Why we march — the future is the quest

Underneath the geopolitics is something every young person feels at the kitchen table: the spread has never felt wider — the cost of living climbing on one side, entry-level wages that have stayed stubbornly flat on the other, and the decisions that shape both being made by whoever showed up. Nobody is coming to hand this generation its future. It gets claimed — by people who show up informed.

The Trap

Costs up, voices ignored

When the cost of living eats the paycheck, there's nothing left to build a life on — and when a generation stays quiet, the people who decide never have to listen. That's not a personal failure. It's a turnout outcome — and turnout can be changed by people who show up informed.

The Future

Decided by who shows up

Every policy that touches a young life — wages, prices, war, debt — was voted on by somebody. The only question is whether this generation is in the room when it happens. The roadmap is simple: register, learn the record, make a plan, and cast the vote. The future gets shaped either way — so shape it.

Opportunity

Leaders you chose

Win the battle today and what follows isn't a prize handed down — it's leaders you chose and empowered, answerable to the people who put them there, and a generation's hand on the wheel of its own future. That starts with one played card: yours.

For families, for the future: this game was made by a father and husband for his two college-age and recently-graduated kids — and for every young person in their band. The point was never fear. It's kinship: learn together, vote together, build a life together.

The field brief — what the game is teaching

The short version of a long night of research, kept honest: facts where the record is documented, judgment labeled as judgment.

1 · The strait is load-bearing

The Strait of Hormuz normally carries ~20 million barrels of oil a day and about a fifth of global LNG, with only ~2.6 million barrels/day of pipeline bypass. When war came in Feb 2026, prices didn't need a total closure to spike — insurers and shipowners pulling out closed it commercially. U.S. gas went from $2.98 (Feb 28) past $4.50 by May.

2 · Tariffs were already in the prices

New York Fed research put tariffs at +2.9 points of consumer-goods inflation by Feb 2026 — before the first strike. A tariff is a tax collected at the border and largely passed to you. Landed cost = price + freight + insurance + tariff + delay. In 2026, every term in that equation rose at once.

3 · Ask who built the corner

Under the 2015 JCPOA deal, Iran's nuclear “breakout” time was ~12 months, inspected. The U.S. withdrew in May 2018; Iran then escalated in announced steps — stockpile up, enrichment to 60%, inspectors out — until breakout was weeks. That compressed timeline was then cited as the emergency requiring war. The facts were real. The authorship was erased.

4 · The second-order hits

  • Fertilizer: ~⅓ of global shipments transit Hormuz — food prices lag the shock by months.
  • Helium & chips: Gulf-linked helium feeds semiconductor fabs; delays idle whole lines.
  • Rates: the 10-year Treasury pushed past 5.1%, mortgages stayed above ~6.3%, hiring and homebuying froze. Buffers — inventories, spare capacity — are finite and already drawn down.

Price surge — or wage-price spiral? The watch list

  • Temporary surge: headline inflation up, but core and services stay contained, and long-term expectations stay anchored.
  • Spiral warning: core + services inflation accelerate for months, across many categories at once.
  • Unit labor costs: wage growth minus productivity keeps climbing — firms price for expected future costs.
  • Expectations unanchor: 5–10 year inflation expectations stay high even after energy stabilizes.
  • The test that matters: several of these together — not one scary headline.

What the midterms actually control

  • The power of the purse: Congress votes the supplemental war funding and the defense budget. No funding, no blank check.
  • Tariff oversight: Congress can challenge executive tariff authority, force exemptions, and reclaim trade power.
  • War Powers & oversight: resolutions, hearings and subpoenas raise the cost of open-ended escalation.
  • The per-candidate rule: party color alone earns nothing. A candidate who votes for unconditional war funding or tariff escalation hasn't earned your vote — check the record, not just the label.

The moment he breaks, the arena goes silent. The drums stop mid-beat. The carousel stalls on its track, its excuses hanging crooked in the sudden quiet — and then, piece by piece, the machinery of The Fade simply stops, the way a storm stops: not with a bang, but with stillness.

And the band is standing in it. All three. Maya on her feet, bow lowered. Dre upright, the Axe of Freedom grounded like a walking staff. Priya with the Sword of Youth point-down, her light steady. Around them, the friends they rallied — neighbors, coworkers, first-time voters — close in, not as an audience, but as part of the line.

Then they walk off. Not running. Not ascending. Walking — in a line, unhurried — off the field and down the road home, carrying what they know, the cards they played, and each other.

What waits ahead is the future this fight was always about, fulfilled the only way it ever is: the changes they battled for, carried now by leaders they empowered — chosen by them, aligned with what they fought for, and able at last to act. Leaders they chose, empowered by the people they serve. Work that pays what a life costs. A town and a country where every voice counts, because every voice showed up.

The future was never his to keep. It was always theirs to claim — and today, informed and together, they claimed it.
